title: Where Does Exactly-Once Live? Model, Harness, and Tool-Contract Effects on Duplicate Side Effects in LLM Agents

claims.claim: (a) simulated services, 12 fault modes, 9 models, 25,930 episodes
claims.evidence: Abstract: 'a deterministic sandbox of six services ... and twelve fault modes injected at the service boundary ... Across 25,930 episodes spanning nine recent models, three production agent harnesses, two contract variants and fifteen recovery conditions'. Note: the GitHub README (jaxblack/limbo-bench) lists only 8 named fault modes; the paper says 12.

claims.claim: (b) proves no verification-only policy is exactly-once under late commits without an in-flight bound
claims.evidence: Abstract: 'We prove that no verification-only policy is exactly-once under late commits without a bound on in-flight time.' Body, Proposition 1: 'No verification-only policy can be exactly-once under late commits without a known bound on in-flight time'.

claims.claim: (c) idempotency keys cut duplicates from about 28% to 4%
claims.evidence: Abstract: offering an idempotency key on every write 'lowers the duplicate rate from 28% to 4% because agents use keys when they exist'. This is a counterfactual contract in which every write accepts a key ('Under a counterfactual contract in which every write accepts one ... the duplicate rate falls from 28% to 4%').

claims.claim: (d) a client-side guard helps weak models only
claims.evidence: Body (HTML): 'For frontier models the prompt-level and harness-level mitigations help little, because these models already verify: the strongest model reaches 77% EOS in vanilla and 77% with the guard.' and 'The guard matters where models are weakest: mai-code-1.1-flash rises from 59% to 76%'. The paper says frontier gains are 'little', not none. Saying 'weak models only' goes further than the paper. The abstract separately says 'a guard that attaches keys transfers across harnesses unchanged'.

claims.claim: (e) an outcome oracle caps client-side policies at 87% on the native contract
claims.evidence: Body (HTML): 'The outcome oracle, which also sees in-flight requests, reaches 87%; 95% of the 105 episodes in which it still produced a duplicate were redelivery on writes without key support, which no client can prevent.' (EOS on the native contract).

notes: The arxiv.org/abs page would not render through the fetch tool. Metadata confirmed from arxiv.org/html/2609.29095 (title, author, affiliation Microsoft, dated September 2026) and from an aggregator listing of the abstract. The exact v1 submission day was not confirmed. Code: https://github.com/jaxblack/limbo-bench (v1.0 release).

title: When Tool Calls Succeed but Workflows Fail: Anomalies at the Agent-Tool Boundary

claims.claim: Effect-history model with anomalies (duplicated, missing, orphaned compensation, residue, ...)
claims.evidence: Abstract: 'We contribute an effect-history model that separates events in the external world from the runtime's observations of them, and a catalog of eight recurring external-effect anomalies.' The catalog has A1 Duplicated Effect, A2 Missing Committed Effect, A3 Orphaned Compensation, A4 Uncompensated Residue, A5 Premature Externalization, A6 Contaminated Speculation, A7 Conflicting Externalization and A8 Phantom Compensation.

claims.claim: Argues no protocol is both unknown-safe and compensation-safe without an authoritative-outcome primitive
claims.evidence: Sec. 4.2: 'Without a primitive that establishes one authoritative outcome (idempotent re-issue returning the original outcome, a status endpoint, or a durable acknowledgment), no protocol can both resolve the workflow after an ambiguous tool call and guarantee unknown-safe and compensation-safe execution.' Note the added condition 'resolve the workflow after an ambiguous tool call'. Sec. 3.1 defines unknown-safe as A1-A3 and compensation-safe as A4.

Abstract: 'measuring the use of the standard annotation vocabulary across 98,291 tools exposed by registered Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers ... none of the required capabilities is fully expressible.' Body: 9,234 remote servers, snapshot 2026-07-27; 74.0% of tools serialize at least one annotation field and 61.7% serialize all four.

notes: Submitted 14 Sep 2026. Comments: 11 pages, 4 tables. Artifact: github.com/flame-stream/mcp-annotation-census. The title uses an en dash in the HTML version ('Agent–Tool Boundary').

claims.evidence: Abstract: 'We introduce a counterfactual benchmark in which every experimental unit pairs these two hidden commit states behind an identical agent-visible timeout.'

title: ACRFence: Preventing Semantic Rollback Attacks in Agent Checkpoint-Restore

claims.claim: After checkpoint-restore, agents re-synthesize slightly different requests causing duplicate effects
claims.evidence: Abstract: the 'retried call will be identical to the original' assumption 'fails for LLM agents, which re-synthesize subtly different requests after restore. Servers treat these re-generated requests as new, enabling duplicate payments, unauthorized reuse of consumed credentials, and other irreversible side effects; we term these semantic rollback attacks.'

notes: v1 21 Mar 2026. Names two attack classes, Action Replay and Authority Resurrection.

title: Beyond Single-Use Tokens: Durable Authorization State for Replay-Resistant LLM Agent Actions

claims.evidence: 'Across 10,152 valid trajectories, agents produce 4,036 semantically equivalent reproposals, yielding an overall rate of 39.8%.' The trajectories cover four uncertain-outcome conditions: lost acknowledgements 58.0%, timeouts 46.0%, ambiguous results 31.0%, delegation/restart 24.0%. The 39.8% is the aggregate over these conditions and three model families.

'each authorization follows an atomic Issued->Prepared->Committed protocol'; at prepare, the system 'allocates k=H(nu||j||tool)', a stable idempotency key. The paper states: 'We introduce CapLease, an authorization-consumption layer for tool-using agents.'

claims.evidence: Page title 'Idempotent requests', https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests. Quotes: 'Stripe's idempotency works by saving the resulting status code and body of the first request made for any given idempotency key, regardless of whether it succeeds or fails. Subsequent requests with the same key return the same result, including 500 errors.' 'You can remove keys from the system automatically after they're at least 24 hours old.' 'The idempotency layer compares incoming parameters to those of the original request and errors if they're not the same.' 'All POST requests accept idempotency keys.' Keys may be up to 255 characters.

claims.claim: Temporal: activities may execute more than once
claims.evidence: Page 'Activity Definition | Temporal Documentation', https://docs.temporal.io/activity-definition. Quotes: 'You should always make your business logic Activities idempotent in Temporal. Because Activities may be retried, these functions may be executed more than once.' and 'For an Activity with a Retry Policy that allows retries, Temporal guarantees that the Activity will be observed as completed exactly once. However, the Activity may be executed multiple times'. Related page: 'What is a Temporal Retry Policy?', https://docs.temporal.io/encyclopedia/retry-policies.

Page 'Workflows | DBOS Docs', https://docs.dbos.dev/python/tutorials/workflow-tutorial. Quotes: 'Steps are tried at least once but are never re-executed after they complete.' 'Transactions commit exactly once.' 'An assigned workflow ID acts as an idempotency key: if a workflow is called multiple times with the same ID, it executes only once.' The 'Steps | DBOS Docs' page does not itself state the guarantee.

They are not guaranteed to provide a faithful description of tool behavior' and 'Clients should never make tool use decisions based on ToolAnnotations received from untrusted servers.' idempotentHint: 'If true, calling the tool repeatedly with the same arguments will have no additional effect on the its environment ...
